metric.why: PPAs are how the boom finances new generation and how operators back renewable claims. Nuclear agreements, including restarts and small modular commitments, became the signature deals of the AI era.
metric.definition: Long-term contracts by which operators secure generation, nuclear, solar, wind, or gas, for current and future facilities.

reading.body:
Power purchase agreements are how data center operators finance new generation, and nuclear deals, including restarts and small modular commitments, became the signature contracts of the AI era.

The definition spans nuclear, solar, wind, and gas, and covers both current and future facilities. That range is the point. An operator signing a PPA is buying firm output rather than a particular fuel, and the contract can be written against a facility that does not yet exist. The commitment runs ahead of the load it serves.

For AI this is the mechanism that turns a demand forecast into revenue a generator can borrow against. Compute capacity is downstream of power, and new generation is difficult to build without a buyer holding a long-term contract. The sibling metrics mark the other half of the problem. Interconnection queue position and wait, approval to energize versus queued load, capacity market clearing price, and behind-the-meter generation all describe whether contracted power can reach a site. A PPA settles who pays for generation, not whether the grid can connect it.

What the data does not contain is any quantity. There are no megawatts, no contract durations, no counterparties, no prices, and no count of agreements signed. It defines a category rather than measuring it, so it cannot show how much of the AI buildout is contracted this way, or whether nuclear's share of those contracts is rising. The statement that nuclear agreements became the signature deals of the AI era is characterization, not a figure supported here.
